following their death. "Beneficiary" means the person or persons designated by the enrollee at
the time of enrollment to receive the plan's benefit; this synthetic plan does not model a

spouse, then children, then parents. "Covered accidental injury" means bodily harm caused by a
sudden, unexpected external event, distinct from a decline caused by an underlying illness or
degenerative condition, and is the category of death exempted from the plan's standard 30-day
waiting period described above. "Contestability period" means the 24-month window from the
enrollment's effective date during which the plan reserves the right to deny a suicide-related
death claim, as described under Exclusions above; the term is specific to the suicide exclusion
and is not used elsewhere in this synthetic plan to describe any other timing rule. "Effective
date" means the date recorded on the enrollment record as the start of active coverage, which is
also the anchor date used to calculate both the 30-day waiting period and the 24-month
contestability period described in this document.

The Group Life Plan pays eligible claims up to a maximum of $10,000.00 per claim. This synthetic
plan does not scale the benefit by salary multiple, age, or tenure — every active enrollee
carries the same flat $10,000.00 benefit cap, unlike many real-world group life products that
tie the benefit to a multiple of annual salary or reduce the benefit amount as an employee ages
past a certain threshold. A claim requesting more than $10,000.00 is denied in full against this
cap rather than paid up to the maximum, and the plan does not prorate the benefit based on how
long the enrollee had been covered before death, how much premium had been paid in, or the
enrollee's age at the time of death. There is no separate accidental death multiplier or
supplemental rider modeled in this synthetic plan, so an accidental death claim is evaluated
against the same flat $10,000.00 cap as any other covered death, without an additional
accidental-death-and-dismemberment benefit layered on top the way a real group life product
often structures a distinct AD&D rider. When a claim names multiple beneficiaries, the
$10,000.00 total is divided among them according to the percentages the enrollee specified at
enrollment, or divided equally if no percentages were specified, but the combined payout across
all named beneficiaries for a single covered death still cannot exceed the $10,000.00 cap. A
beneficiary designation left blank or naming a beneficiary who predeceased the enrollee is
handled outside this synthetic plan's automated cap rules and instead requires manual review, since
the plan does not model a default-beneficiary hierarchy, as described further under Definitions
below.

A newly enrolled employee's coverage under this plan is subject to a 30-day waiting period from
the enrollment's effective date before any claim becomes eligible, mirroring the waiting period
applied uniformly across this synthetic plan's other lines of coverage. No waiting period is
applied to death resulting from a covered accidental injury sustained after the effective date,
meaning a fatal accident such as a traffic collision or an accidental fall occurring on day five
of coverage is still eligible for the full benefit, since accidental deaths are, by construction,
not foreseeable at the time of enrollment and do not present the anti-selection risk the waiting
period is designed to guard against. Death from a pre-existing terminal illness diagnosed before
the enrollment's effective date, by contrast, remains subject to the full 30-day waiting period
and is not treated as an unforeseeable accidental event. An employee who re-enrolls after a lapse
in coverage restarts the 30-day waiting period in full, regardless of how long they were
previously enrolled before the lapse, and regardless of whether the lapse was voluntary or caused
by an administrative processing delay. The waiting period runs independently of, and is not
combined with, the 24-month suicide contestability period described under Exclusions above; a
death within the first 30 days of enrollment is evaluated against the waiting period first, and
only a death that clears the waiting period is then checked against the contestability period
and the other exclusions. A death occurring precisely on the 30th day of coverage, counting the
effective date itself as day one, is treated as having cleared the waiting period rather than
falling one day short of it.

"Active coverage" means an enrollment record with status `ACTIVE` as of the date of service, not
the date the claim was submitted, meaning coverage that lapses between the date of service and
the date of filing does not retroactively invalidate an otherwise eligible claim. "Preventive
service" means routine cleanings, exams, and x-rays performed at intervals consistent with
standard dental care guidelines, such as a cleaning and exam roughly every six months. "Basic
service" means fillings, simple extractions, and prescribed night guards for diagnosed
conditions — procedures that address existing decay or damage without the higher cost or
complexity of a major service. "Major service" means any procedure involving a crown, bridge,
root canal, dental implant restoring chewing function, or extraction beyond a simple tooth
extraction, and is the category subject to the plan's extended 90-day waiting period described
above. "Simple tooth extraction" means removal of a fully erupted tooth visible above the gumline
without the need for bone removal or sectioning, as distinguished from a surgical extraction of
an impacted tooth, which this plan classifies as a major service. A procedure not clearly falling
into one of these three categories is classified by the claims team based on the treating
provider's procedure code at the time of adjudication, using standard industry procedure-code
groupings rather than the provider's own informal description of the work performed. "Date of
service" means the calendar date the procedure was actually performed and billed, which is the
anchor date used throughout this document for the active-coverage check, the late-filing window,
and the major-service waiting period alike.

A newly enrolled employee must wait 30 days from the enrollment's effective date before any
dental claim becomes eligible for benefits. Major services (crowns, bridges, root canals, and
extractions beyond a simple tooth extraction) carry an additional waiting period of 90 days from
the effective date, reflecting the higher cost and lower urgency of these procedures relative to
preventive care — preventive care and basic services such as fillings and simple extractions are
not subject to this extended waiting period, since encouraging early routine visits is
consistent with the plan's broader cost-management goals even during the initial enrollment
window. A member who switches from an individual dental plan directly into this group plan does
not receive credit toward either waiting period for time already served under the prior
individual plan, and a member re-enrolling after any lapse in this group plan's coverage restarts
both waiting periods from zero regardless of how long they were previously covered. A procedure
that begins as a basic service but is upgraded mid-treatment to a major service, for example a
filling that reveals the need for a root canal once the tooth is opened, is evaluated against
the major-service waiting period based on the date the major service was actually performed,
not the date the original, lower-tier procedure was scheduled or begun. A multi-visit major
service, such as a crown requiring a preparation visit followed by a separate cementation visit
several weeks later, is treated as a single claim measured against the 90-day waiting period
using the date of the first visit in that course of treatment, and is not split into two claims
evaluated against two different waiting-period snapshots. If an employee's waiting period would
otherwise end mid-procedure — for example, a root canal begun one week before the 90-day mark
and completed one week after it — the claim is evaluated as of the date the completed procedure
was billed, so the claim is treated as eligible in that scenario rather than denied for having
started before the waiting period technically closed.

Cosmetic dental procedures, including teeth whitening and veneers placed for appearance rather
than function, are excluded from coverage, even when a treating dentist frames the procedure as
having some incidental functional benefit such as improved bite alignment from veneer placement.
Orthodontic treatment for members over the age of 19 is excluded, as this synthetic plan treats
adult orthodontia as elective regardless of whether the treatment addresses a bite alignment
issue with functional consequences like jaw pain or uneven wear. Claims for treatment received
outside a licensed dental provider's care, or for over-the-counter dental products such as
whitening strips, store-bought mouthguards, or night guards purchased without a prescription for
diagnosed teeth grinding, are not covered; a custom night guard prescribed by a dentist for
diagnosed bruxism is covered as a basic service. Dental implants placed purely to replace a
missing tooth for cosmetic reasons, as opposed to restoring chewing function after an accident
or extraction necessitated by decay, are excluded from this synthetic plan's benefit. Any claim
submitted more than 180 days after the date of service is denied for late filing, and this
window is measured from the date service was rendered, not the date the provider's invoice was
issued, the date the member received an explanation of benefits, or the date the member became
aware of the out-of-pocket cost. Treatment received from a provider outside the member's home
state or country while traveling is not automatically excluded on that basis alone, provided the
provider holds a license recognized by the jurisdiction in which the treatment was performed and
the claim is otherwise filed within the standard 180-day window.

"Active coverage" means an enrollment record with status `ACTIVE` as of the date of service, not
the date the claim was submitted, so coverage that lapses after the date of service but before
the claim is filed does not retroactively disqualify an otherwise eligible claim. "Eligible
vision claim" means an eye exam performed by a licensed optometrist or ophthalmologist, or
prescription eyewear (glasses or contact lenses) issued pursuant to a current prescription no
more than 24 months old at the time of purchase, reflecting the plan's assumption that
prescriptions older than that are unlikely to still accurately reflect the member's vision.
"Contact lens fitting fee" means the charge for the exam and follow-up visits needed to
determine the correct lens curvature and fit, distinct from the base eye exam fee, but treated
as part of the same eligible claim when billed alongside contact lenses rather than as a
standalone service. "Lens upgrade" means an optional feature added to standard corrective
lenses, such as anti-glare coating, photochromic tinting, or a progressive (no-line bifocal)
design, and is treated as part of the same eligible claim as the base lenses rather than a
separate line item subject to its own cap. "Frames" means the physical structure holding the
lenses, evaluated as part of the same combined eyewear claim as the lenses themselves; a member
who purchases frames only, intending to reuse lenses from a prior pair, may still file a claim
for the frames alone under this same benefit.

The Group Vision Plan reimburses eligible vision claims up to a maximum of $500.00 per claim.
This limit covers eye exams, prescription eyeglasses (frames and lenses), lens upgrades such as
anti-glare coating or progressive lenses, and contact lenses in combination, not as separate
sub-limits, in this synthetic plan — a member who needs both an exam and new eyeglasses in the
same visit files one claim covering both, still capped at $500.00 total rather than $500.00 per
item. A claim requesting more than $500.00 is denied in full against the plan's cap rather than
partially reimbursed up to the limit, and the plan does not average the exam cost separately
from the eyewear cost, or the frame cost separately from the lens cost, to bring any individual
component under the cap on its own. There is no separate annual aggregate cap beyond the
per-claim limit, so a member who needs a second, unrelated vision claim later in the same plan
year, for example a lost-and-replaced pair of glasses or a new prescription following a change
in eyesight, files it as an independent claim evaluated on its own merits against the full
$500.00 limit again. A contact lens fitting fee charged separately from the lenses themselves is
treated as part of the same claim as the lenses it relates to, not as a standalone eligible
expense, and is included in the total measured against the cap.

Laser vision correction surgery (LASIK and similar refractive procedures) is excluded from this
plan, as it is treated as an elective procedure rather than corrective eyewear, even when a
member's optometrist recommends it as a long-term alternative to glasses or contacts. Safety
glasses or protective eyewear required for a member's job duties are excluded from this personal
vision benefit, since such equipment is expected to be provided or reimbursed separately by the
employer as workplace safety equipment rather than personal health coverage. Non-prescription
(cosmetic-only) contact lenses and sunglasses without a corrective prescription are excluded,
since the plan's purpose is to offset the cost of vision correction rather than eyewear in
general, though prescription sunglasses used as a member's only pair of corrective eyewear are
covered under the standard eyeglasses benefit. Replacement eyewear purchased solely for style
rather than due to a change in prescription or physical damage is not covered, and a member
cannot file a second claim for replacement frames within the same plan year absent a qualifying
prescription change or a documented damage event such as a broken frame. Claims submitted more
than 180 days after the date of service are denied for late filing, measured from the date of
purchase or exam, not the date the invoice was paid or the date a payment plan for the eyewear
was completed. Eyewear purchased through an online retailer using a prescription issued by a
provider outside the plan's typical network is not excluded on that basis alone, provided the
prescribing provider is licensed and the prescription is current under the 24-month rule
described under Definitions below.

"Active coverage" means an enrollment record with status `ACTIVE` as of the date the claim's
underlying disability began, not the date the claim was submitted — a claim can therefore be
denied for lack of coverage even if the member's enrollment was active at the moment of filing,
if it had lapsed or not yet begun on the actual date of disability onset. "Short-term
disability" means an inability to perform the material duties of the employee's own occupation,
meaning the specific job the employee held immediately before the disability began, for a period
expected to last between 14 and 180 days; this plan does not apply the stricter "any occupation"
standard some disability products use after an initial period, under which a claim could be
denied if the member could perform some other, different job. Disabilities expected to last
longer than 180 days fall outside this plan's scope and are not addressed by this synthetic
document, since a real long-term disability product would typically be structured as a separate
plan with its own eligibility rules, elimination period, and benefit schedule. "Material duties"
means the core functions of the role as described in the employee's job description at the time
the disability began, not incidental tasks the employee may have occasionally performed outside
that description. "Elimination period" is a term used in some disability products for the
window between disability onset and benefit eligibility; this synthetic plan uses the simpler
term "waiting period" throughout and does not distinguish the two concepts separately.

The Group Disability Plan reimburses eligible short-term disability claims up to a maximum of
$5,000.00 per claim. Claims requesting more than this amount are denied automatically by the
plan's benefit cap, regardless of the underlying medical circumstances, the treating provider's
recommendation, or how compelling the supporting documentation is. The requested amount is
generally calculated as a percentage of the member's regular wages for the period the member was
unable to work, capped at the plan's weekly benefit schedule; the plan does not reimburse lost
bonuses, commissions, or overtime pay that would have been speculative rather than guaranteed.
There is no separate annual aggregate cap beyond the per-claim limit in this synthetic plan —
each claim is evaluated independently against the $5,000.00 ceiling, and a member who files
several claims within the same plan year, for example one claim for a short illness in the
spring and an unrelated claim for a minor injury later in the year, is not subject to a running
total across those separate claims. Partial reimbursement up to the cap is not offered; a claim
requesting more than $5,000.00 is denied in full rather than paid up to the maximum, since the
plan is not designed to auto-adjust a requested amount downward to fit within the benefit cap.
A claim spanning a partial work week is prorated based on the number of scheduled work days
missed, rounded to the nearest whole dollar, and this proration happens before the cap is
applied, not after. Members are encouraged, though not required, to itemize the basis for the
requested amount when submitting a claim, since a clear itemization can help the claims team
distinguish a legitimate high-cost claim from a data-entry error, even though it does not change
how the cap itself is applied to the final requested figure.

The plan does not cover disabilities resulting from self-inflicted injury, participation in an
illegal act, or a pre-existing condition diagnosed and treated within the 90 days immediately
before the enrollment's effective date. Disability arising from normal, uncomplicated pregnancy
is covered under a separate maternity rider and is excluded from this plan's base benefit,
meaning a claim filed for pregnancy-related disability under the base plan will be denied even
though a nearly identical claim filed correctly under the maternity rider might be approved.
Disability arising primarily from a diagnosed substance use disorder is excluded unless the
member was enrolled in an approved treatment program at the time the disability began, in which
case the claim is evaluated under the plan's standard rules rather than being excluded outright.
Cosmetic procedures and any disability arising directly from a cosmetic procedure are excluded
entirely, including complications from an elective cosmetic surgery performed outside the
member's home region, and including recovery time from a procedure the member describes as
medically motivated if a licensed provider classifies it as cosmetic. Disability sustained while
engaging in a hazardous recreational activity not disclosed at enrollment, such as skydiving,
scuba diving beyond recreational certification limits, or professional-level motor racing, is
excluded, though ordinary recreational activities like hiking, cycling, or amateur team sports
are not considered hazardous for this purpose. Claims submitted more than 180 days after the
date of disability onset are denied for late filing, independent of medical eligibility — the
plan treats the 180-day filing window as a hard administrative boundary rather than a guideline
subject to case-by-case exceptions, even when the delay was caused by the disability itself.
